layers.title: In the browser
layers.lede: Everything anyone using the tool does: read the design, set the inputs, run, keep what a run returned, and ask for a node to change. **Nothing in the browser changes the design.** What you set and what you keep are yours and stay on your machine; what the design *is* changes only through a node's form, which the developers check, apply and release.

sections.title: Open the tool
sections.answer: Start the tool with one command and open the address it prints. It never writes the repository: what you keep — the case and your results — stays on your machine under ~/.vleo.
sections.body:
The tool is one program on your own machine. It serves this page and computes every number on it, from one address, with no internet and no database. It listens on `127.0.0.1` only, so nobody else on the network can reach it.

**It never writes the repository.** The two things you can keep — the case you run on and the results you save — are kept outside it, under `~/.vleo/`, so a checkout stays exactly as it was released and `git status` is empty however much you use the tool. The status card at the top of this manual says where this copy keeps them.

steps.say: Start it. It prints the address it got — the first free port from 7777 upward.
Open the address it printed, normally `http://127.0.0.1:7777`.
In a Codespace there is nothing to type: the tool is already running and port 7777 opens as a preview.

Without a repository, the tool comes two ways. The one file for every laptop: `python -m pip install vleo-<version>-py3-none-any.whl` once, then `python -m vleo` — it runs inside Python, so Windows has no new program to stop. Or a kit, the zip for your system: double-click `Start VLEO.exe` on Windows, or run `./start.sh` on macOS and Linux. Either opens the page itself; `START_HERE.md` says the rest.

sections.title: Who does what
sections.answer: Five roles, and one loop until the switch-over. The programme manager, the system engineer, each subsystem engineer and each node engineer own the design and use the tool; when a node is wrong or missing, its node engineer fills its form, tries the preview of the change and approves it. The developer takes each form in, sends the preview, records the approval and releases — and writes what that routine cannot: code, checks, the tool itself. Each role has a deputy who may act for it.
sections.body:
The line between the roles is the line between *owning and using* the design, *moving a change through*, and *building the machinery*. The design's own roles follow the tree: the **programme manager** owns the management side, the **system engineer** the whole spacecraft and the one release everyone works from, each **subsystem engineer** their group's branch, and each **node engineer** their nodes (`docs/OPERATING_1_0.md`, section 2).

**Everyone uses it.** Anyone can set the inputs — by hand or as a CSV — run any row on them, save what the run returned and send it on, and look at a result somebody else saved without running anything. When a node is wrong, missing or unfinished, its node engineer — the person who knows the answer — fills in **that node's form** and sends it. They get a **preview** of their change back, try it, and press **Approve** — or say what is still wrong.

**The developer moves each change through, until the switch-over.** A form that arrives is taken in onto its own branch — checked, applied, tested — and the node engineer who filled it is sent the preview. Their approval comes back as a file, and is recorded against exactly the build they tried. Approved changes are merged, and released to everyone when the developer chooses. Every step is one command. From the switch-over on there are no forms: each owner signs their own files in the application, and the developer maintains only the code.

**The developer builds the machinery.** A form that adds a relation needs code in the kernel; a check that fails for a reason not in the form needs a diagnosis; the tool's pages, pictures, checks and generators are designed and improved. All of it through the gate and a reviewed pull request.

There are three guides — for the engineers, `docs/roles/user.html`; for intake until the switch-over, `maintainer.html`; and for the developer, `developer.html` — generated from this manual, so the three can never disagree with it.

sections.title: Find your way around
sections.answer: The design is a tree of rows in four layers, drawn with its connections on one grid. Pick a layer, open a group, click a row to open its page.
sections.body:
The design is a tree of rows in four layers. Each row asks one small question and has one answer. The tabs across the top are the layers, plus the architecture every row repeats.

The big figure shows two things on one grid. The **tree** runs down the diagonal: a group is a box, a row is a cell. The **connections** are the marks: a row's own row of the grid is what it feeds, its column is what feeds it. Click anything and its inputs light up one colour and what it feeds another.

Click a group's cell on the diagonal to open it, and again to close it. Or open everything at once.
Click a row's cell to open that row's own page.
From the keyboard: the **up** and **down** arrows move the selection, **left** and **right** open and close a group, **Esc** goes back to the layer.
First time? The tool explains its own figure.

sections.title: Read a row
sections.answer: A row's page opens with its answer first, then says it simply, then the real relation and its source, then where the simple version breaks. Every claim says whether it is sourced, derived or declared, and the depth switch chooses how much is shown.
sections.body:
A row's page answers four questions, in order.

**What it is made of** — the files in its folder, which one a person writes (`node.toml`, the sheet) and which ones are generated from it.

**What it is joined to** — the rows it reads, the rows that read it, and which customer targets it feeds.

**What it says** — the sheet itself, laid out the same way on every row: an **Answer first** box, then the row **said simply**, then **the real thing** — its relation and where that came from — then **where the simple version breaks**, and the wrong idea readers most often bring. Every claim is marked *sourced*, *derived* or *declared*, and every tab says whether it is an explanation, a reference or something to try. The **de-risking** tab says what the row rests on and why it changed. Beside the sheet is the node's **form**, for when what it says should change.

**The picture** — for the rows that have one, the figure the claim is argued from.

A **grey** row is *seeded*: its folder exists and nothing is specified in it yet. That is the normal state of most of the tree — the decomposition written down before anyone was asked to fill it — not a failure, and its form is how it gets filled. A row marked **INACTIVE** has a relation but nothing on its sheet saying where the relation came from, so it does not answer until a form supplies that and a developer applies it.

sections.title: Set the inputs — the case
sections.answer: Every run is on one case: its inputs, set on the Inputs page or uploaded as a CSV and saved outside the repository. A file is shown before it is saved, refused whole if any row is bad, and carried over when the tool is updated.
sections.body:
There is **one case**, the multipayload design, and every run, sweep and figure in the tool is for it. What changes from one customer to the next, or from one sky to the next, is its **inputs** — never the tree. A customer is a set of values, not a folder, so a new customer is never a change to the design.

The **Inputs** tab lists all of them in two halves. **Condition** is what the design flies in: the orbit, the environment and the solar weather it is sized for. **Customer** is everything else — the payloads, the vehicle, the service and what it must deliver. Each shows the value it runs at, its default — the value declared on its own sheet — and the range it may move in.

Change values there and save them, or **upload a CSV**. A file is read and shown before anything is saved: what it sets, what that changes, and every row it refuses. A file with any refused row — a name that is not an input, a unit that is not the row's, a value outside the declared range — is not used at all, because keeping the good half would be a run on values nobody asked for. A blank value means the default, so a file only has to name what it changes.

The saved case is kept by the tool **outside the repository** — beside the reference data, in `~/.vleo/case/`, or wherever `VLEO_CASE` points — so git never sees it. To keep a copy, or hand one to someone, download it; to put it back, upload it. The bar across the top always says how many inputs the saved case changes.

**When the tool is updated, a case carries over.** Every CSV the tool writes names the set of inputs it was written for, in a `#! template` line — keep it. When a release adds, retires or re-ranges inputs, a case written before is not refused: every value that still applies is carried, every new input runs at its default, and any value that can no longer be used — its input retired, or now outside its range — is **set aside** by name, with its value and why, rather than dropped. The saved case is carried over on its own the first time the updated tool reads it, and the file as it was is kept beside it; the Inputs page says what the update did until you keep the result. An old file you upload is carried over the same way, and shown before it is saved.

Change a value, then save. **default** puts one input back.
Or start from the template — every input, every value blank — fill it in anywhere a table can be edited, and upload it.
Upload a CSV. What it would change is shown first; nothing is saved until you say so.
Save the file as the case, or discard it.
Keep a copy of the case as it stands.

sections.title: Run a row, and ask “what if”
sections.answer: Run any computed row on the case, or change an input first to ask what if. A run always says how many rows ran and names every one that was blocked.
sections.body:
Every computed row can be evaluated on the spot, on its own page or from the **4 The run** tab.

**A run is on the case** — its saved inputs, see *Set the inputs*. The panel says so in a sentence, and under it lists every input the answer depends on, the most influential first, each with the value it will run at, which half of the case it is in, and where the value came from: the **default**, the **saved case**, or **your edit**.

**Change one to ask a what-if.** The edit is kept in this browser only — listed in the bar at the top, applied to every run and sweep until you reset it, and never written to a file. A **computed** row cannot be changed this way: its value would be recomputed from its inputs the moment it ran, so change one of the declared numbers it reads instead. When a what-if is worth keeping, **save it to the case** and every page runs on it from then on.

The result always says **n ran, m blocked**, and names every blocked row. A row with nothing in it does not quietly supply a default — it refuses, under its own name, and everything that needed it says so. That count is never hidden, because a number built partly on refusals is not the number it looks like. What unblocks such a row is its form, filled and applied — see *Ask for a node to change*.

sections.title: Keep a result, send it, and see it again without running
sections.answer: Save a run or a sweep as a result, and see it again later without running anything — or send its report page. A question already answered is not run again: the tool shows the saved answer and says so. A result keeps the node versions it rested on, and says when one of those beliefs has broken since.
sections.body:
A run is worth keeping when somebody will ask about it later. **Save** it and the tool keeps a **folder**: `result.csv` — every value the run returned with its unit, its credibility and what governs it, every row it blocked on and why, and **every input it ran on** — `sweep.csv` when it is a sweep, and `report.html`, the page to send. It is kept in `~/.vleo/results/` or wherever `VLEO_RESULTS` points — outside the repository, like the case.

**A question already answered is not run again.** Everything that decides an answer — the row, how much of the graph, every input, the engine, the tree and the reference data, and for a sweep what it moved and how — is one key. Press **run** or **sweep** on a question already kept and the saved answer is shown, with a line saying which result it came from and when; **run again anyway** runs it fresh. Saving the same question twice keeps it once. With `VLEO_RESULTS` on a shared folder, that includes questions a colleague answered. A change to the engine's code or to the tree is a different key, so an answer from before a correction is never shown for the corrected tool.

The **Results** tab lists every saved result and shows any of them as it was — **nothing runs**, so a result saved before a release reads exactly the same after it. Two results can be compared value by value, and the inputs that differ between them are listed first, because that is usually the answer.

A saved **sweep** is drawn again on the Results page from its saved points, with the same chart the run panel uses — hover, zoom and copy the numbers — and nothing runs.

To send one, download its **report**: one HTML page that reads without the tool, draws the sweep, and carries the CSVs inside it, so uploading the report gives the result back whole. The **CSV** opens in any spreadsheet. A result somebody sent you is uploaded the same way: its report, or its `result.csv` with its `sweep.csv`.

**Results are kept in tiers.** Every value for 30 days — `VLEO_KEEP_DAYS` sets how many — and the summary for good: when the tool starts, an older result is thinned to the inputs it ran on, its answer and what could not run, and says so on its page and in its report. The rest is one run away, because the same engine on the same inputs gives the same answer; a thinned result is not offered as a kept answer, so asking its question again runs it. **Pin** a result to keep every value of it for good. A shared folder named by `VLEO_RESULTS` is kept whole unless `VLEO_KEEP_DAYS` is set too.

**A result's inputs can become the case.** That puts every input back to what the result ran on — the way to reproduce it, or to carry on from it. It is checked like any other case, and refused whole if a release has since retired or re-ranged something it sets.

sections.title: Ask for a node to change, or for a new one
sections.answer: To change a node, or ask for a new one, download its form, fill it anywhere and send it to the developers. If the change moves what the node computes, the form also says why: which belief broke, what was tested and what we now know.
sections.body:
Every node has a **form**: one self-contained HTML file that needs no connection and nothing installed. It explains itself, asks every question the node's sheet answers with *why* each is asked, shows what the node reads and feeds and the known-good values that already hold it, lists every row it could read, and saves a filled copy of itself. Send it to whoever should say what the node is — a payload team, a customer's engineer, a reviewer. It can be filled by hand, or given to an assistant: the content is a plain block of text near the end of the file.

**For a node the design does not have yet**, download the form for a new node. It also asks where the node goes — its parent, and so its layer — and what kind of row it is.

**What it reads is its interface.** Every input names a row that exists, and the form says, as you type, what that row is and its quantity. A developer's first check is exactly this: that every input is a row, of the quantity the node expects.

**Why it is changing.** A change to what the node computes — an input, the output, the model, the maths, the algorithm, how it is drawn — also says which belief broke: what we believed, what we tested, what we now know, what changes, and what the node rests on now. The form says as you type which decisions your changes move and what is still to answer; without it the developers apply only your wording. Wording alone needs none of it.

Send the filled file to the developers. **This page can check it first** — what it would change in the node, every interface it declares, and what cannot be applied: a field the design changed since the form was made is a *conflict*, never overwritten, and a relation an assistant supplied is *refused*, because mathematics is derived by a person. Nothing is written here. Known-good values in a form are passed to whoever records fixtures; they are never written from a form.

steps.say: Every form in one place: the inputs, results, and each node's form.
Or from a node's own page: in *the sheet*, open the form tab.

sections.title: Give the method, your code and your test cases
sections.answer: In a node's form, write the relation once more as a method — a few lines in a small fixed language — paste the code you wrote and tested, and give at least three cases your code answered and one it refuses. The form runs your method on your cases as you type and shows any that disagree, before you send it.
sections.body:
A node's relation arrives three ways, and each checks the other two. **Your code** — MATLAB, Python, C, anything — produced your test cases. **The method** says the same relation in the method language (docs/PSEUDOCODE.md), which the tool can check for units and run. **The code the tool ships** is generated from the method. All three must give your answers, so a mistake in any one of them shows up as a case that disagrees.

**The method.** It reads the node's inputs by their names, gives every number its unit in brackets — `250 [km]`, `30 [deg]` — and ends every path with `return` (the answer) or `refuse` (why it will not answer). The form checks the units as you type: adding a length to a time, taking the logarithm of a length, or returning the wrong quantity is shown on the line it happens.

**Your cases.** Each is a set of inputs, in SI, and the answer your code gave for them, with how close counts. At least three answers and one case the node must refuse — the refusal shows the method says no where your code says no. The method's value appears beside yours only after you have typed yours, so the tool is never where your answer came from.

**Your code and its test** are pasted whole, with what ran them. They are kept with the node so the cases can be produced again and a reviewer can read where the numbers came from.

**Flight software** that implements the node can be kept in the same form, each file with its test and its last result. It is stored beside the relation, not built by the tool.

Every question has **Show the example** beside it: the same question answered for one worked node, marked illustrative.

steps.say: Open the node's form and find *The method*. Read *The method language on one page* if it is your first.
Write the method, then fill *Your code*: the code, its language, the function that is this node, and the test code that ran it.
Add your test cases — three or more with the answer your code gave, and one it refuses — and watch *Check: the method against your cases* until it says **Sound**.

sections.title: Try the preview of your change, and approve it
sections.answer: After you send a form, you get a preview of the tool with your change in it. Install it, try the nodes it names, and press Approve only when they give what you expect; send back the small file it saves. Nothing reaches everyone else until you do.
sections.body:
A **preview** is the tool built from your form, before the change is approved. It is the same one-file package as a release, and it says so on every view: an orange **PREVIEW** banner names your change, the nodes it touches and the build. Install it exactly like a release, over the one you have — your inputs and results are kept, and the next release replaces the preview.

Open each node the banner names, read its page, run it, move its inputs, and check the answers against your own. **If anything is wrong, do not approve** — tell the developer what, and you will get a new preview. When it is right, press **Approve this preview…**, tick that you ran it, and save the file. Send that file back the way you sent the form.

The file is for this build and no other: if anything changes after you approve, you are sent a new preview to approve.

sections.title: Why a node changes — its beliefs, versions and risks
sections.answer: A node changes only because a belief it rested on broke, and every change records what we believed, what we tested, what we now know and what changed. The risk-register rows of the management layer conclude, from every node's record, how that work has moved the programme's risks.
sections.body:
Every decision in the design rests on a belief — that this relation holds here, that this input is the one that matters, that this picture shows what it claims. A node changes only when one of those beliefs **breaks**: somebody tested it and learned otherwise. So a node's page has a **de-risking** tab. It says what the node rests on now and what would break it, then every version before it, newest first: what we believed, what we tested, what we now know, what it cost, what changed, and which risks that moved.

`sw_central_expectation` — the centre of the F10.7 design value — carries its real history as the worked example: three versions, each replaced because a test showed its belief did not hold.

**The conclusion is drawn in the management layer.** A risk is registered once, on one of the four risk-register rows — technical, schedule, supply, regulatory — and moved only by node versions. Each of those rows' pages lists its risks, where each started and where it stands now, and every version across the tree that moved it. That is how the work below, taken together, has de-risked the programme; `docs/DERISK_NARRATIVE.md` is the same thing as a document, and `docs/derisking.csv` as a spreadsheet.

**A saved result keeps the versions it rested on.** When one of those rows has moved on since, the result says so beside its number.

**How deep a page goes is yours to choose.** The switch at the top — **Learn**, **Read**, **Expert** — shows the same pages at three depths: Learn keeps every step and asks you to predict before you run; Read shows the answer, the plain words and the real thing; Expert keeps the answer, the relation, the limits and the reference. How every page is laid out, and why, is in `docs/EXPLAINING.md`.

Open a row and its de-risking tab: what it rests on now, and every version before it.

sections.title: What the browser will not do
sections.answer: The browser never changes the design. Each thing it will not do has a place it is done instead, and for anyone using it that place is almost always a node's form.
sections.body:
The browser never changes the design: not a field, not a row, not the tree. That is not to keep anybody out. A change to the design has to be checked against every row that reads it, implemented, given evidence, and released so that everyone runs the same thing — and a change typed into one copy of the tool does none of that. So each one below has a place it is done instead, and for anyone using it that place is almost always a form.

The fields a node form does not carry at all — the ones that move a row in the tree or change who owns it — are listed live under *Reference*, each with its reason.

layers.title: Maintaining the repository
layers.lede: The routine that moves every change from a node form to everyone's copy: take the form in, send the node engineer who filled it a preview, record their approval, merge, release, share. **Every step is one command**, and each does its whole step or nothing and says what to do next. Nothing here writes code — what needs code goes to a developer, with the output that says why.

sections.title: The loop, and where each change stands
sections.answer: Each form lives on its own branch, form/<name>/<node>, and passes through four stages: taken, previewed, approved, merged into the `maintainer` branch. main only ever receives changes whose node engineer tried and approved them, through a pull request from `maintainer`; a release takes everything merged into main since the last one.
sections.body:
**Taken.** `take` checks the form and, if it can be applied, puts it on its own branch from a fresh `maintainer` — applied, regenerated, gated, tested, committed with the node engineer's name, pushed. If it cannot, it writes a note to send back and changes nothing.

**Previewed.** Every push to a form branch builds a preview by itself: the tool with this one change in it, marked PREVIEW on every view. You send it to the node engineer who filled the form.

**Approved.** They try it and press Approve; the file it saves names the exact build. `approve` records it on the branch — refused if anything has changed since that build — and the pull request's approval check turns green.

**Merged, then released.** You merge the pull request into `maintainer` when every check is green. When a set of changes is ready, a pull request takes `maintainer` into `main`; `ship` cuts a release from main when you choose; the release pipeline builds the four files; you publish and share them.

Many forms can be in flight at once, each on its own branch, none waiting for another. `queue` says where each one stands.

steps.say: Where every form branch stands right now.

sections.title: Take a node form in
sections.answer: Save the form you received into forms/, then run take naming its node engineer. It either puts the change on its own branch — applied, tested, committed, pushed — or writes a note to send back and changes nothing.
sections.body:
`forms/` at the top of the repository is where received forms and the notes sent back live; git ignores it, because the form is its node engineer's and is attached to the pull request rather than committed.

`take` refuses to start with uncommitted changes, so nothing of yours is swept into a commit that names somebody else. It then works in numbered steps — the branch, the form applied, everything regenerated, the gate, the tests, the commit and push — and stops at the first that fails, saying which and how to abandon the branch. A test that fails is a physics question for the node's owner, never a tolerance to change.

**Not taken** means a field conflicts with a change made since the form was downloaded, an input is not a row of the right quantity, or a relation came from an assistant. The note says which, field by field; send it back, and take the corrected form when it returns — with `--again` if its branch exists.

sections.title: Take a group's sealed release in
sections.answer: A group sends a sealed release instead of forms. Unpack it, read what group-intake says, then apply, build, test and deliver it on the branch group/<group>-<version>. It merges only with the group's acceptance of the test application.
sections.body:
The release is checked against its seal before anything is read: one byte changed and it is refused, and the fix goes back to the group as a note. Each computed node then becomes the form its node engineer would have filled, and goes through intake's own check.

**Not taken** means a conflict with a change made since, an incomplete de-risking record, or a method or results an assistant supplied. A node whose declaration says `transcribed` is taken only when it names the source the method was copied from and the person who read the copy against it; without either, or with an assistant as the checker, it counts as one an assistant supplied. A transcription is still reviewed at H1b against its source, by someone other than the person who signed it.

`group-test` holds the build to the group's own results. A disagreement is physics, for the group — never a result or tolerance moved to pass.

sections.title: Check a node's method against its node engineer's cases
sections.answer: Run method with the node's id. It checks the method and runs every one of the node engineer's cases through it — the same check the node engineer saw in their form, and the one the gate refuses on.
sections.body: `take` prints the same check before it applies a form, under *the method, against the node engineer's cases*, and the gate refuses a node whose method does not check, whose cases disagree, or that has fewer than three answers and one refusal. A case that disagrees is the node engineer's to settle — their code, their method or their expected value is wrong — so it goes back to them with the line printed, never to a tolerance.

steps.say: Check one node's method and cases.
steps.why: prints each case with what the node engineer's code gave and what the method gives, or says the node has no method yet

sections.title: Build a node from its method
sections.answer: take does this for you when a form carries a method; build-node does it by hand. Every stage must pass before the next runs, and the node is connected to the rest of the design only at the end.
sections.body:
**M** the method runs on the node engineer's cases. **G1** the method is translated, by fixed rules, into a kernel function in `vleo-core::physics::methods` — the node's code calls it and has no holes. **T1** the node, guards and all, must reproduce every case; **T2** the translation must give the method's own answer to the last bit, around every case. **T3** the node engineer's own code is run again where it can be. **T4** the answer is moved on purpose and the tests must notice. **I1** only then is the node checked in the tree, and the rows that read it are named.

A case that fails is the node engineer's to settle. A translation test that fails is a translator defect, for a developer. Neither is ever a tolerance to change.

steps.say: Rerun every node engineer's code on the cases recorded from it.
steps.why: says, per node with cases, whether the node engineer's code still gives them, or why it could not be run here

sections.title: Move the design over to methods, a batch at a time
sections.answer: Run migration to see which rows still need a method and whose they are; with --forms it writes each owner's node forms into one folder. Send them; each comes back through take like any other change.
sections.body: Nothing breaks meanwhile. A row without a method keeps its hand-written code and its gap list says *no method yet*; a row with one is built from it and tested against its owner's cases. A method is mathematics, so it only ever comes from the node's owner — never from this command, and never from an assistant. A row that answers a set of values keeps its holes: the method language answers one quantity.

sections.title: Send the node engineer a preview
sections.answer: The push from take builds the preview by itself, in about ten minutes. Download it from the newest green preview run, unzip it once, and send the .whl inside to the node engineer.
sections.body:
The preview is the one-file Python package a release ships, built from this branch, with Windows and Linux engines. Its version carries `+preview.<author>.<build>`, so it is never taken for a release, and every view shows the PREVIEW banner with the Approve button.

**Node engineers on a Mac:** the macOS engines cost ten times the build minutes, so they are built only when asked — Actions → preview → Run workflow → the branch → *also build the macOS engines*.

**How the file travels is yours to choose.** Whatever channel you use, send the `.whl` itself, not a link that needs a GitHub login.

steps.say: Where this branch's preview is. On main it refuses: previews are built for form branches.
Open the newest green **preview** run for the branch, download `vleo-preview-<author>-<build>` at the bottom of the page, unzip it once, and send the `.whl` inside.

sections.title: Record the node engineer's approval, and merge
sections.answer: Run approve on the file the node engineer sends back. It is recorded only if it is for the build of exactly what is on the branch now; then the pull request can be merged once every check is green.
sections.body:
**Refused, and why that is right:** the file is for an older build (anything pushed since — a fix, main merged in — needs a new preview and a new approval); the node engineer did not tick that they ran it; the file is not an approval at all. Each refusal says which.

**The pull request.** `take` and `approve` both print its link. Merge only when every check is green — among them **the author approved this exact change**, which reruns the same check the pipeline's way. Use *Squash and merge*: the node engineer's `Form-by:` line and the approval travel with it into `maintainer`, and on into main.

An approval is a record, not a password: it proves which build was approved, and you, who received it, vouch for who sent it.

steps.why: stores it in approvals/ on the branch, commits naming the node engineer, and pushes

steps.why: reads only; shown as not run because it needs a form branch to name

sections.title: Release a version
sections.answer: Once maintainer and developer are merged into main, run ship on an up-to-date main. Merge the pull request it opens the way to and tag the merge commit; the release pipeline builds and publishes the four files itself.
sections.body:
`ship` cuts `release/<version>`: the de-risking narrative regenerated, every node version still marked `next` stamped with this release, regeneration, the gate, the tests, one commit, pushed. It lists whose forms the release carries.

**The merge is the decision.** The release workflow builds only a commit that a merged pull request put on main, and refuses anything else before it builds (docs/RELEASE_SETUP.md). After the merge, tag the merge commit (the commands `ship` prints). The **release** workflow then builds the three kits and the one-file package, installs the package on Windows, macOS and Linux, and publishes the release with the four files attached; share the `.whl` with everyone.

Choosing the number: the middle number for new behaviour or a change in how everyone gets the tool, the last for fixes.

sections.title: When a form changes what a node reads or feeds
sections.answer: take prints every input the form declares and whether it connects. A change to what a node reads or feeds can move other nodes' answers, so find who reads it and send those owners the preview too.
sections.body: The interface check at take is the same one intake runs: each input names a row that exists, of the quantity the node expects. A form that re-points an input or changes a node's output is still one node's change, but its answers travel: `reach` shows where each answer goes, and CODEOWNERS names who owns the nodes downstream. Send them the same preview; an approval from the node engineer who filled the form covers their node, and the downstream nodes' engineers' word covers theirs.

steps.say: Where each answer goes, and which reach no KPI closure.

sections.title: Two forms for the same node
sections.answer: Each still gets its own branch. Merge the first when it is approved; then bring maintainer into the second, send its node engineer a new preview, and record their new approval.
sections.body: Two node engineers can send forms for one node at once — each is taken onto its own branch, and neither waits. After the first merges, the second is behind maintainer. Bring maintainer into it (`git switch form/<author>/<node>` then `git merge origin/maintainer`); if the same field changed in both, git stops with a conflict — that is a question for the two node engineers, never a coin toss, and a developer can resolve it once they agree. Anything pushed after an approval needs a new preview and a new approval, so the second author approves the combined change.

sections.title: Worked example: one form, start to finish
sections.answer: Ana sends a form for sw_ap_design. It is taken onto form/ana-sharma/sw-ap-design, previewed, approved, merged and released — five commands and two files exchanged. (Illustrative: the steps and messages are real, the people are not.)
sections.body:
**1 · The form arrives.** Ana's filled `sw_ap_design.node-form.html` is saved into `forms/`. `take … --for "Ana Sharma"` prints each change it applies, runs the gate and the tests, commits *feat(mod-solar): sw_ap_design from a node form* with `Form-by: Ana Sharma`, pushes, and prints two links.

**2 · The preview.** Ten minutes later the preview run is green. Its package `vleo-preview-ana-sharma-7` holds one `.whl`, sent to Ana.

**3 · Ana tries it.** The banner reads *PREVIEW of Ana Sharma's change to sw_ap_design · build 7 · not a release*. She runs the node, checks it against the NOAA table she used, presses Approve and sends back `vleo-approval-ana-sharma-build7.toml`.

**4 · Recorded.** `approve` on that file prints *approved. Ana Sharma approved build 7*. `queue` now shows the branch as *approved — review and merge*. The pull request's checks are green, among them *the author approved this exact change*; it is squash-merged.

**5 · Released.** When a few forms are merged, `ship 0.3.0` cuts the release, its pull request is merged, `v0.3.0` is tagged on the merge commit, and the release workflow publishes the four files. Ana installs 0.3.0 over the preview; her inputs and results are still there.

**What would have stopped it:** had Ana's form re-pointed an input to a row that does not exist, take would have written the note to send back and changed nothing; had a fix been pushed after build 7, approve would have refused her file and asked for a new preview.

sections.title: What goes to a developer
sections.answer: Anything that needs code or judgement about the machinery: a form that adds a relation, a check that fails for a reason not in the form, a merge conflict, a change to the tool itself. Hand over the command and its output.
sections.body:
**A new relation.** A form for a new node, or one that changes its maths, can need a function in the kernel and a filled HOLE. take applies the form; `declare` and `publish` then say what code is owed — a developer's step.

**A failing check that is not the form's.** The gate or a test fails on the form branch for a reason in another node, a generator or the pipeline. The output names it; hand it over with the branch.

**A merge conflict** between two forms, once their node engineers agree.

**The tool itself** — its pages and pictures, the commands in this layer, the checks, the release pipeline. Those are code, reviewed as code.

layers.title: In the terminal
layers.lede: Paste these from the top of the repository. Each command is marked with what it does: the ones marked **safe to run** only read, and the pipeline runs every one of them exactly as written here and holds it to what this page says it prints. The ones marked **changes files** are not run by the pipeline — they would change the repository it is checking — but their names and flags are still checked against the programs themselves.

sections.answer: Install Rust, clone, wire the hooks once and fill the reference-data store once. Then the gate and the tests are the one command that must be green.
sections.body:
The only thing to install is Rust; the exact version is pinned in `rust-toolchain.toml` and fetched on first use. There is no database and no service.

`setup` points git at the project's own hooks so the commit-message rule runs before a bad message ever leaves your machine. Git will not do this on its own, because a hook that ran just because it was cloned would be a way to run anybody's code.

Every command here is written out in full. Two shorter forms work too: `cargo xtask …` for `cargo run -p xtask -- …`, and `cargo vleo …` for `cargo run -p vleo-cli --bin vleo -- …`.

sections.title: Run, change an input, sweep, keep the result
sections.answer: Run a row on the case, on a CSV of your own or on the declared defaults, change a declared input with --set, sweep one, and keep a run as a result file.
sections.body:
The examples use the storm row `sw_ap_design`: *what daily Ap is this design built to survive?* It reads one declared number, the storm level designed for, and turns it into the Ap that level bounds.

A run prints the answer, its **credibility** — the weakest of eight factors, named — and **n ran, m blocked** with every blocked row named. The **chain** hash identifies that exact number: the engine, the tree and every input that reached it. Two runs with the same chain are the same run, so it is the thing to quote.

A run is on the **case**: the saved one — the same file the browser saves — or, with `--inputs`, a CSV of your own, or with `--defaults` every input at its declared value. The first lines of a run say which. `vleo inputs` prints the case as a CSV to fill in; a blank value means the default, and a file with any row that cannot be applied is refused whole, each bad row named. A file written by an older version of the tool — its `#! template` line says so — is carried over instead, and `vleo inputs --inputs old.csv` writes it out in the current template, with every value it could not carry kept as a `#! set-aside` line. The order is fixed: each row's declared value, then the case's, then `--set`.

`--set` only changes a **declared** number — never a computed one, which would be overwritten the moment it was evaluated — and it never writes the sheet.

`--save` writes the run as a **result** file where you say; `--keep` keeps it in the results folder the browser's Results page shows, once. A question already kept there is shown from its saved result instead of run — the first line says so — and `--again` runs it anyway. `vleo result` shows a result again, from its folder, its CSV or its report, without running anything.

Two of the steps use a **closure**, `l3_solar_ach_01`: the room the sustained F10.7 requirement has left once the design flux is taken from it. The launch date is one of the declared numbers behind it, and a time is given in seconds.

sections.title: Take in a node form — check it first
sections.answer: A developer's first act on a filled form is the checker, which writes nothing: what it would change, every interface it declares, what cannot be applied, and whether its reason is complete. Then --apply writes it as one edit, or not at all.
sections.body:
Every change to the design arrives as a node's form, filled by whoever knew the answer. A developer's first act on one is to **check** it, and nothing is written by checking. `xtask intake` reads the filled file and says, field by field, what it would change in the node's `node.toml`, against three versions: the node when the form was made, what the filler made of it, and the node now — so a change made in the repository meanwhile is a **conflict**, not overwritten. It checks **every interface** the form declares: each input must be a row that exists, or a named output of one, of the quantity the node expects. A relation an assistant supplied is **refused**, and so is a numbered step removed from the middle, because each number is a hole holding somebody's Rust.

A form for a **new node** says where it goes. Intake checks that the id is free and the parent is a group, and on `--apply` builds the folder in its place in the tree — on the shape of a sibling of the same kind — then writes the form into it and gates the **whole tree**, since a new row changes what the tree connects. Anything the form left blank is listed as still open.

`--apply` writes as one edit — regenerate, gate, and put everything back if the gate refuses — with your name on any relation it changes. It refuses while anything is blocked unless you add `--partial`. Known-good values in the form are printed as `[[fixture]]` blocks for whoever records fixtures; they are never written by intake. A filled seeded row is then **published**, which is what generates its code — see *Implement a node*.

steps.say: A node's form, to send out. With `--out <file>` it is written to a file.
The form for a node the design does not have yet.
Check a filled form — this one changes the note, adds an assumption and supplies a known value.
Check a filled form for a new node: where it goes, what it would hold, and each interface it declares.
Apply it: written, regenerated and gated as one edit, or not at all. Then read `git diff`.

sections.title: Implement a node — the developer's loop
sections.answer: After a form is applied: publish the row so its code is generated, write the Rust in each numbered slot, add evidence from outside this code, and check it. Every step names exactly what is still open.
sections.body:
A row is a folder, and **only `node.toml` in it is written by hand** — by a form's intake, or in your editor. Every other file is generated from it; an edit anywhere else is thrown away the next time the row is regenerated, and the checks catch it before then.

The loop after a form is applied: publish the row so its code is generated, write the few lines of Rust in each numbered slot, give it evidence from outside this code, check it, and ask whether a person should look yet. Every step names exactly what is still open, so there is never a guess about what is next.

**Any assistant may help write a slot.** `fill` takes the body as text, and `--by` and `--model` record who wrote it and with what, so a significant slot written twice by different models can be compared. What no assistant may supply is the relation itself — that comes from the form, and a person's name goes against it. Commit naming whoever filled the form.

sections.title: Record why it changed, and cut a release
sections.answer: Every applied change appends a version to its node; the narrative is regenerated from all of them; and a release stamps every unreleased version with the release that ships it.
sections.body:
A form that moves what a node computes carries its reason — what we believed, what we tested, what we now know, what changed, and what the node rests on now. Intake checks the record with everything else: without it, only the form's wording is applied and every decision is **withheld**, by name; with it, the changes go in and a `[[version]]` is appended to the sheet, numbered and marked `next`. The kinds of decision it moved are read off what the form changed, never asked. A risk move names a risk registered on a risk-register row, or the record is refused.

The narrative is generated from every node's record: `docs/DERISK_NARRATIVE.md` to read and `docs/derisking.csv` for a spreadsheet, in the columns of the quarterly de-risking narrative. The pipeline regenerates both and fails on a difference.

A release names the beliefs it ships. `xtask release <version>` stamps every `next` with the release, sets the workspace version and regenerates; the release pipeline runs `release <version> --check` and refuses while any version is unstamped. Why, and the rules, are in `docs/DERISKING.md`.

sections.title: What a command does, where it stopped, and why a node is what it is
sections.answer: Every xtask command is described in one table: explain prints a command's place in a node's journey, what it reads, writes and checks, how to undo it and where its code is. A command that writes prints numbered steps, says why it stopped and how to retry, leaves a trace, and takes --dry-run. why puts a node's history in one place.
sections.body:
**One table describes every command** — `xtask/src/pipeline.rs`. `explain` prints it for one command, or the whole journey with none; `docs/PIPELINE.md` is the same table as a page, regenerated by `xtask pipeline`; and a test fails when the table, `help` and the code disagree.

**A command that writes runs as numbered steps** — `take`, `intake --apply`, `publish`, `fill`, `build-node`, `release` and `ship`. Each step prints `n/total · name` as it starts and what it found when it ends. A step that stops prints **why**, the state the **files** are in, the exact command to **retry**, and the **code**: the file, and the step's name — a string in that file, so searching for the printed name finds the line.

**Every such run leaves a trace** in `target/xtask-trace/` — the command line, the commit, each step with its time and result. `xtask trace` shows the last one, `trace <command>` the last of one command, `trace --list` every one kept (the newest 50).

**--dry-run, on any command that writes**, does nothing: it runs the command's own check where it has one (`intake` without `--apply`, `release --check`, `method-wasm --check`, `pipeline --check`), and otherwise prints the plan — its steps, what it would write, how to undo it.

**why <node>** answers "how did this node come to be this?": every recorded version and who made it, the commits that changed it, its approvals, how its code came to be, and its gate, run now.

steps.say: The whole journey, and the command at each step.
One command: where it sits, what it reads, writes and checks, how to undo it, and where its code is.

A node's history in one place, and its gate now.

sections.title: Work on the page without the engine, and change what they share
sections.answer: The page and the engine meet at one contract in contract/: every route, a schema for every answer, the file formats, and answers recorded from the real engine. A frontend developer runs the page on the mock engine with no Rust; a backend developer proves the engine keeps the contract with cargo test. Inside /v1 a change may only add.
sections.body:
**The contract is `contract/`** — `routes.toml` lists every route and the requests the tests make; `schemas/` has one schema per kind of answer; `formats/` the CSV files people keep and send; `examples/` answers recorded from the real engine. `contract/README.md` is the whole of it.

**The backend keeps it.** The contract tests start the real server and make every request: every answer must validate against its schema, and a field the schema does not declare is a failure — so the page may read only what the contract lists. They run in `cargo test`.

**The frontend builds against it.** `tools/mock_engine.py` serves the page from `web/` and every answer from the recorded examples, with no Rust built; the page says **MOCK ENGINE** at the top, because every number on it is an example. `tools/mock_check.py` walks the page on it in a browser, and the pipeline runs that with no Rust toolchain at all.

**Changing it.** Within `/v1`, add only: a new route or field breaks nobody. A field goes into the schema first, in a pull request both sides review; then either side can use it. Removing or re-meaning one is `/v2`, beside `/v1` for a release. When an answer's shape changes, re-record the examples. The page carries the contract version it was built for and names an engine that speaks another.

The page on recorded answers, with no Rust — then open the address it prints.

sections.title: Take a lesson in, from its form
sections.answer: A lesson arrives the way a node change does: the node engineer who knows the row fills its lesson form anywhere, checked as they type by the gate's own check, and sends it back; lesson apply checks it again, writes lesson.toml beside the row's node.toml and gates the row — or puts it back.
sections.body:
The node engineer writes the lesson; nobody writes HTML for it and nobody writes a formula for the page to compute. `docs/LESSONS.md` is the file, table by table, and `docs/examples/orbit_velocity.lesson.toml` a complete example.

**The form** is one HTML file — from `lesson form`, or *write a lesson — its form* on the row's page. It carries the checker every node form carries, which holds the lesson check the gate runs, and a table of the tree's rows, so a widget naming a row that is not there is refused while the node engineer types. **lesson check** says what a filled one holds and every reason it would be refused; **lesson apply** writes it and gates the row, and puts the row back if the gate refuses. A lesson is outside the sheet hash, so it never changes an answer.

steps.say: A row's lesson form, to send to whoever knows the row.
steps.run: cargo run -p xtask -- lesson form orbit_velocity --out orbit_velocity.lesson-form.html

sections.title: Share the tool with everyone
sections.answer: Everyone gets the tool, not the repository: one Python package for every laptop, or a kit per platform — the programs beside exactly the files they read, with START_HERE.md on top. They use it and send back node forms; you apply them, release, and share the next version.

Zip it and share it. A kit runs on the platform that built it; the release pipeline builds one for Linux, macOS and Windows, and one Python package, `vleo-<version>-py3-none-any.whl`, that carries the engine for every system and runs with `python -m vleo` — no new program for Windows or an antivirus to question. Each person's case and results live under `~/.vleo/`, outside both, so the next version replaces them without losing either. The whole loop is in `docs/SHARING.md`.

sections.title: The method language and the form's checker
sections.answer: The method language is one module, vleo_sheet::method. Every node form carries it compiled to WebAssembly as web/method.wasm.gz; after changing the language, rebuild that file with method-wasm and commit it with its stamp.
sections.body: The gate, `take`, intake and the node form all call `vleo_sheet::method` — the form through `web/method.wasm.gz`, which `xtask method-wasm` builds from `crates/vleo-method-wasm`. A test refuses a checkout whose checker sources have moved on from the committed file, so a form can never check by older rules than the gate. A form reads the file from beside the tree when it is made; no program carries it built in, because compressed WebAssembly inside a program is what Chrome blocked in the first 0.3.0 Windows kit, and the release refuses a program that does. `docs/PSEUDOCODE.md` is written by `xtask docs` from the same tables the checker reads. Changing what a method means is a reviewed change to every node that has one.

sections.title: When the method language cannot say it
sections.answer: A node the method language cannot express — a set of answers, a solver that stops when it converges — keeps hand-written holes. A developer writes them, with an assistant if they like, and the node engineer's cases still decide.
sections.body:
The language is closed on purpose: every construct has one translation, so the translator needs no judgement. What it cannot express goes to the existing route: `fill` splices each hole body, `--by` and `--model` record who wrote it, and a **significant** node's holes are written twice by different model families and compared with `differential`. An assistant here is a worker, never a judge: acceptance is only ever the node engineer's cases, the fixtures, the mutation check and the gate — and no assistant supplies the relation, the method or a case.

When the language grows a construct, it grows in `crates/vleo-sheet/src/method.rs` and the files under `method/` beside it — the grammar (`parse.rs`), the checker (`check.rs`), the interpreter (`run.rs`) and the translation (`rust.rs`) together, one reviewed change, followed by `method-wasm` so every form checks by the new rules.

sections.title: Before you push, and how to release
sections.answer: Run the pipeline's checks before pushing: the gate and every test first, then formatting, lints, the assembly validations and the panels. A change from a form names who filled it.
sections.body:
The pipeline runs all of these on every push; running them first saves a round trip. The first is the one that must be green.

Commit messages read `type(scope): a sentence saying what changed`. The hook installed by `setup` refuses anything else before it leaves your machine, and the pipeline runs the same rule. A change that came from a form names who filled it. How many reviewers a change needs is in `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

Once merged, the change reaches everyone in the next release: they update, and their saved case carries over on its own — see *Set the inputs*.

The commit types and every valid scope.

Every value crossing that boundary is in SI units; a face converts for display, never for transport. The full list of routes is under *Reference*. **No route writes the repository**: the only things a request can save are the case and results, both kept outside it.

sections.title: When something goes wrong
sections.answer: The usual failures, each with what it means and what to do. Almost every refusal names the field and the rule, and that line is usually the whole answer.
sections.body:
**The tool will not start: nothing was free.** It tries sixteen ports from 7777 upward. Something else is holding them — often an earlier copy of the tool. Stop that one, or set `VLEO_PORT` to start somewhere else.

**An uploaded case or result is refused.** Every refused row is named, with why. A case is all or nothing, so correct the named rows and upload it again. A file from an older release is carried over rather than refused; one the tool did not write — no `#! result` line — is not a result at all.

**A form's check shows a conflict.** Somebody changed that field in the design after the form was made. Nothing is overwritten: download the node's form again, carry the answer across, and send the new one.

**A form's check says an interface does not connect.** The input names a row that does not exist, or one of a different quantity. The line says which, and what the row it names actually is.

**The checks refuse a row.** Each failure names the field and the rule. Read that line before anything else; it is almost always the whole answer.

**A row prints INACTIVE and does not answer.** Its relation is written but nobody has derived it: the sheet has no `[theory]` block saying why it is this relation. That is a person's work, supplied through the node's form, never something to work around — and every row that reads it is blocked, by name, until it is done. `active` lists each such row and how many rows wait on it.

**A sweep answers no point.** Every point is still recorded, with why: *blocked* when a row on its chain does not answer, or the bound and its reason when the value is outside the declared range of the row being swept.

**A command warns that the hooks are not wired.** Run `setup` once in this checkout.

**The commit hook refuses a message.** It must read `type(scope): a sentence`, and `tools/commit_message.py --types` prints every type and scope it accepts.

**A number looks wrong.** Run the row in the terminal, read its credibility line and which factor governs it, and look at *the chain behind this number* — every value that reached it, with each one's own credibility. If the design is what is wrong, that is a form.

steps.say: Start the tool on another port.
Every row that is written but does not answer, and how many rows wait on each.
